question: On 19 February 2024, the Commission announced that it had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Rwanda as part of the Global Gateway strategy. The MoU seeks to nurture sustainable and resilient value chains for critical raw materials, notably tantalum.

Yet according to the NGO Global Witness, 90% of the tantalum exported by Rwanda actually comes from the DRC1, where extraction of such minerals fuels armed groups, notably M23, a movement which is seemingly backed by Rwanda, according to a UN report2. In recent weeks, hundreds of thousands of people have had to flee the hostilities3. 1.

Can the Commission provide the impact assessment carried out prior to the MoU, in particular the figures on the origin of the tantalum exported by Rwanda (including domestic extraction) and the quantity exported (by country)?
Can it clarify the link between the MoU and the Conflict Minerals Regulation?

What steps have been taken to ensure that the tantalum exported by Rwanda was indeed extracted in Rwanda, or legally imported into the country? Will those steps be agreed with civil society in the roadmap that will accompany the MoU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.5.2024) A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) does not create any legal or financial obligations, and as such does not entail the need for a formal impact assessment. It represents an expression of a political will to cooperate in a certain domain.

Foreseen cooperation stemming out from the MoUs signed with Rwanda and Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) will include increased transparency and traceability of extracted raw materials, which will help counter for example illicit tantalum exports. The MoU and the Conflict Minerals Regulation1 are coherent and have the potential to reinforce each other.

The main objective of the Regulation is to ensure that EU importers of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold buy from responsible sources only, in line with the standards set by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)2.

The EU has been financing the European Partnership for Responsible Minerals3, an accompanying measure to the Conflict Minerals Regulation, while also aims at improving mineral resources management. The programme ‘Peace and Security for Stability in the Great Lakes region’4, which supports the implementation of a Regional Certification Mechanism, also aims at reducing mineral resources impact on conflict.
The Rwanda MoU also supports Rwanda’s engagement within the Extractive Industry Transparency Initiative5.
